explanations.explanation: Isaiah says it right up front: “Behold, a king will reign in righteousness…” That's how this king rules, and it's the whole point. Not by looking impressive, not by being the loudest guy in the room. He reigns the right way, every time.

Splendor is a fair guess, friend. Kings and shiny things go together like me and a fresh batch. But Isaiah never uses that word. He says the king will reign in righteousness, which is about how he rules, not how fancy the throne looks.

A silent king would make for a very quiet palace, but Isaiah doesn't say that. His word for how the king reigns is righteousness. Quiet does show up later, though: Isaiah says the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence (verse 17).
Yes, friend, justice. Isaiah says the king reigns in righteousness and the princes rule with justice. Righteousness at the top and justice right behind it. That's a leadership team I'd sign up for.
Strength feels like a natural pick for rulers. My mustache can lift a whole cookie box, so I respect it. But Isaiah's word for the princes is justice. That's what they rule with.

Wealth would make for some very comfortable princes. But Isaiah doesn't mention it. He says they will rule with justice. I think a prince with a full treasury and no justice is just a fancy cookie tin with nothing good inside.

Streams of water in a dry land. Isaiah puts it right next to “…the shadow of a great rock in an arid land.” I think water and shade mean the most exactly where there isn't any. Think of how good shade feels after a long stretch in a hot kitchen standing next to the oven.
A valley is a good guess, since water likes to settle low. But Isaiah never mentions a valley. He says these rulers are like streams of water in a dry land. The dryness is the whole picture.

A royal garden sounds lovely, friend, and I bet it has plenty of water already. But Isaiah puts the streams somewhere else: in a dry land. Same with the great rock, which gives its shadow in an arid land. He's painting these rulers as water and shade in dry places.
True. Isaiah says the ears of those who hear will listen. Hearing and listening are two different things, friend. I've heard my kitchen timer go off plenty of times and did NOT listen.

It's true, actually. Isaiah says “…the ears of those who hear will listen.” He pairs it with the eyes of those who see no longer being closed. Hearing is one thing, but this is hearing that actually pays attention, like finally catching the timer.
Isaiah says the opposite. He says “The mind of the rash will know and understand…” Not more reckless, but wiser. It's a change for the better, and I'm all for it.

False, and good eye. Isaiah says the mind of the rash will know and understand. The same verse says the stammering tongue will speak clearly and fluently. Rushing in without thinking is something I know a lot about, so this verse makes me smile.

Fool is the word. Isaiah says no longer will a fool be called noble, nor a scoundrel be respected. It comes after Isaiah says a king will reign in righteousness (verse 1). That's a kingdom I'd like to see.

Coward is a decent guess, but it isn't in this verse. Isaiah names the fool and the scoundrel. He says no longer will a fool be called noble, nor a scoundrel be respected. The word you wanted was fool.

Boaster sounds like it could fit, friend, since folks like that love a spotlight. But Isaiah doesn't use that word here. He says no longer will a fool be called noble, nor a scoundrel be respected. Fool is the one.
The hungry. Isaiah says the fool “…leaves the hungry empty and deprives the thirsty of drink.” That's a fool who leaves people in need with nothing. Isaiah doesn't soften it, and neither will I.

The rich would be an odd fit, friend, since they've already got plenty. Isaiah says the fool leaves the hungry empty. The thirsty get deprived of drink in the very same line. This is about people with real needs.

Proud makes sense if you're thinking of a fool with a big head. But Isaiah's word is hungry. The fool leaves the hungry empty and deprives the thirsty of drink. Those are people who just needed something simple and didn't get it.

It's the other way around, friend, and it's a heavy line. Isaiah says the scoundrel “…hatches plots to destroy the poor with lies, even when the plea of the needy is just.” So the plea can be completely fair and he still goes after them. Nothing in the verse gives him an excuse.

False. Isaiah says the scoundrel hatches plots to destroy the poor with lies, “…even when the plea of the needy is just.” Even when. His weapons are destructive, Isaiah says. This is a heavy verse, so I'll just say it plainly: the plea is fair, and he still goes after them.

Worthy it is. Isaiah says the noble man makes honorable plans and “…stands up for worthy causes.” Honorable plans and worthy causes go together in that verse. That's a short sentence with a lot of backbone.
Lost is a kind guess, and it sounds sweet. But the verse doesn't say it. Isaiah says the noble man stands up for worthy causes. The standard is whether the cause is worthy.
Popular, friend? That's the trap. Isaiah says worthy causes, and I think those two words don't always travel together. A flavor everyone's talking about isn't automatically a good cookie.
In just over a year. Isaiah says “In a little more than a year you will tremble, O secure ones.” That's not some far-off day. A year and a bit goes by quick, especially when you're comfortable.
Seventy years is a long wait, friend, and Isaiah doesn't say that. He says “In a little more than a year…” That's a lot closer than seventy. The warning has a short fuse.

Forty days is close, but Isaiah gives a different number. He says “In a little more than a year you will tremble…” So there's a bit more time than that. Still not long, and he says so to the secure ones on purpose.
Fail is the word Isaiah uses. The grape harvest will fail, and the fruit harvest will not arrive. That's a hard year for anyone counting on the vines. Nothing in the verse softens it.
Double would be a happy surprise, friend, but it's the opposite of what Isaiah says. The grape harvest will fail. The fruit harvest won't even arrive. That's why the secure ones are told to tremble.
Ripen sounds nice, like a batch coming out right. But Isaiah says the grape harvest will fail, and the fruit harvest will not arrive. Ripening isn't what the verse describes.

explanations.answer: The pleasant fields and fruitful vines
explanations.explanation: The pleasant fields and the fruitful vines. Isaiah says “Beat your breasts for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vines…” The land itself is what they're mourning. When the harvest goes, that's a loss you can see.

explanations.answer: A king who has fallen in battle
explanations.explanation: A fallen king is a classic reason for mourning, but this passage doesn't mention one. The grief is for “…the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vines…” Isaiah also describes the land of his people as overgrown with thorns and briers (verse 13). The king in this passage is the one who reigns in righteousness (verse 1).

Treasure would sting, friend, but Isaiah doesn't list any. He tells them to beat their breasts for the pleasant fields and the fruitful vines. The grief is for the land that gives the harvest. No chest of gold in sight.

Isaiah says the opposite, friend. He says “…the palace will be forsaken, the busy city abandoned.” That's a palace left behind and a busy city given up. The hill and the watchtower become caves, a delight for wild donkeys and a pasture for flocks.
False. Isaiah says “…the palace will be forsaken, the busy city abandoned.” The hill and the watchtower become caves, and wild donkeys and flocks move in. A busy city gone quiet is a hard picture.

The Spirit. Isaiah says the ruin lasts “…until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high.” That one word turns the whole thing around. After the Spirit is poured out, the desert becomes an orchard.
Rain makes sense, friend, and I think that's why it's tempting. A dry land and a pouring sky go together. But Isaiah says what's poured out from on high is the Spirit. That's the turning point.

Oil gets poured in plenty of places, so it's a fair guess. But Isaiah doesn't say it here. He says the ruin lasts until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high. The Spirit is what changes the land.
True. Isaiah says that once the Spirit is poured out, “…the desert will be an orchard…” Dry ground becomes a place full of fruit. And then he adds that the orchard will seem like a forest.

It's true, friend. Isaiah says once the Spirit is poured out, “…the desert will be an orchard…” It's a big turnaround after all the ruin. And he keeps going, saying the orchard will seem like a forest.

The wilderness. Isaiah says “Then justice will inhabit the wilderness, and righteousness will dwell in the fertile field.” The wild, empty place gets justice, and the fertile field gets righteousness. Both places get named.
A palace feels like where justice should live, friend. But a few verses back, Isaiah said the palace will be forsaken (verse 14). Here, justice inhabits the wilderness. It moves into the open land.
A marketplace could use some justice, I'll give you that. But Isaiah doesn't mention one here. He says justice will inhabit the wilderness. Righteousness gets the fertile field.
Peace is the word. Isaiah says “The work of righteousness will be peace…” And the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever. Doing right ends up in a calm place.
Glory sounds big and bright, friend, and I get the pull. But Isaiah's word is peace. The work of righteousness will be peace. The next line adds quiet confidence forever.
Toil is a good guess if you think righteousness means nonstop sweating. But Isaiah says the work of righteousness will be peace. The service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever.
Isaiah says the opposite. He says “…my people will dwell in a peaceful place, in safe and secure places of rest.” Dwell means they stay. That's the picture of people finally getting to sit down.

False. Isaiah says “…my people will dwell in a peaceful place, in safe and secure places of rest.” They settle in, with safe and secure places of rest. It's the kind of rest I'd take over a hundred cookie orders.

explanations.answer: Those who sow beside abundant waters
explanations.explanation: Those who sow beside abundant waters. That's how Isaiah ends: “Blessed are those who sow beside abundant waters…” Sowing near plenty of water is a smart place to plant, and Isaiah calls those people blessed. And it follows the picture of the Spirit poured out and the land changed.

explanations.answer: Those who build houses on the rock
explanations.explanation: Building on the rock is a real blessing picture, but it's from a different place. Jesus talks about a wise man who built his house on the rock (Matthew 7:24). Isaiah ends this passage somewhere else. He says blessed are those who sow beside abundant waters.

explanations.answer: Those who store grain in barns
explanations.explanation: Barns full of grain sound like a happy ending, friend. But Isaiah doesn't mention barns. He ends with “Blessed are those who sow beside abundant waters…” The blessing goes to the sowers by the water.
